h: Bayleaf, the Gridshell and a working mill
p: Some buildings at the Weald and Downland Living Museum are worth seeking out above others. Bayleaf is a famous timber-framed Wealden hall house, furnished to show how a well-off farming household lived in the early 1500s, and it's a brilliant way to understand how people cooked, ate and slept around an open hearth. Close by, the Tudor kitchen often has food being prepared using period recipes, and the smell alone pulls people in.

The working watermill, rebuilt here from Lurgashall, still grinds flour, which gives a real sense of how villages depended on their mill. Shire horses and other traditional breeds work and graze around the site too, and they're a hit with children. Then there's the striking Downland Gridshell, a modern timber building that houses workshops and collections, so it's a nice bit of contrast against all the old stuff.

Set your pace by the weather. On a sunny day you could spend hours out on the slopes, while on a showery one you'll want to hop between buildings and save the far corners for a dry spell. Bring a picnic, as the downland views are part of the experience.

Singleton is a pretty flint village in the valley of the River Lavant, and the grounds of West Dean, with their gardens and glasshouses, are just next door. Goodwood is over the hill, Kingley Vale's ancient yew woodland is a short drive away for a walk, and Chichester's cathedral, shops and harbour are only a few miles south for an evening out. It all adds up to a corner of Sussex that rewards a long weekend rather than a flying visit.
